Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions

retrieved_chunks.text:
Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: paper_PAPER - Kakumanu et al. - 2024 - Applying the dissemination and implementation sciences to allergy and immunol
retrieved_chunks.text:
Clinical implications:
  - Application of D&I sciences can lead to more consistent delivery of evidence-based practices in asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, drug allergy, food allergy, and primary immunodeficiency by identifying and mitigating contextual barriers.
  - Integrating D&I frameworks into research and practice can help address observed health disparities in minoritized and underserved populations.
  - D&I approaches may improve the uptake of critical interventions such as early peanut introduction, penicillin allergy delabeling, and SMART therapy in asthma.

Practice implications:
  - Allergists and immunologists should be receptive to practice changes informed by D&I study findings and actively leverage D&I research to develop and adapt healthcare interventions.
  - Clinicians and health systems should incorporate D&I frameworks when planning and evaluating the implementation of new guidelines or quality improvement initiatives.
  - Multidisciplinary teams that include community partners, patients, and diverse stakeholders are essential for successful D&I efforts.
  - Guideline developers should consider including implementation strategies and D&I principles to facilitate real-world adoption.

Limitations:
  - D&I studies can be expensive, particularly when multiple sites are involved, and may face competing operational pressures within health systems.
  - The variety of available D&I frameworks can be daunting, and selecting the most appropriate one requires expertise.
  - Without careful integration of a health equity lens, D&I research risks exacerbating existing disparities by favoring populations with greater access and health literacy.
  - The need for mixed methods, longitudinal data, and real-time EHR or digital data collection adds complexity to study design and execution.

Strengths:
  - D&I sciences provide a rigorous, systematic methodology to study not only clinical effectiveness but also reach, adoption, implementation fidelity, and sustainability of evidence-based practices.
  - The use of process, determinant, and evaluation frameworks (e.g., EPIS, CFIR, RE-AIM) offers structured roadmaps to guide implementation and assess contextual factors.
  - Mixed methods approaches allow for a comprehensive understanding of barriers and facilitators at individual, organizational, and system levels.
  - D&I research explicitly prioritizes health equity and can uncover how interventions affect historically marginalized populations differently.

      Allergy and immunology ebp: Atopic dermatitis guidelines41; Atopic Dermatitis Workgroup Report 202242

    Row 4:

Condition or topic: Allergic rhinitis

Clinical background: Allergic rhinitis is commonly managed with intranasal or oral medications. Current guidelines, such as ARIA 2020, suggest intranasal treatments for moderate-to-severe disease, citing faster onset and higher effectiveness, but the certainty of evidence for these recommendations is often low or very low. Similarly, the US 2020 Practice Parameter recommends intranasal corticosteroids as first-line therapy without detailed comparisons with oral options. Existing head-to-head studies have employed heterogeneous outcome measures and inconsistent methodological rigor. Recent high-quality systematic reviews on this topic are absent; the last comprehensive review was published in 1998 and limited to intranasal corticosteroids versus oral antihistamines, while a later review imposed language and date restrictions. An updated evidence synthesis is required to support the 2024 revision of the ARIA guidelines.

Objectives:
  - To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the effectiveness of intranasal corticosteroids or intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists in improving nasal and ocular symptoms and quality of life in allergic rhinitis.
  - To assess the safety of these interventions by evaluating adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events.

Clinical question: In patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis (P), how do intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) (I) compare with oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists) (C) in improving total nasal symptom score, total ocular symptom score, and rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life (O)?

Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions

Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

Clinical implications:
  - Application of D&I sciences can lead to more consistent delivery of evidence-based practices in asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, drug allergy, food allergy, and primary immunodeficiency by identifying and mitigating contextual barriers.
  - Integrating D&I frameworks into research and practice can help address observed health disparities in minoritized and underserved populations.
  - D&I approaches may improve the uptake of critical interventions such as early peanut introduction, penicillin allergy delabeling, and SMART therapy in asthma.

Practice implications:
  - Allergists and immunologists should be receptive to practice changes informed by D&I study findings and actively leverage D&I research to develop and adapt healthcare interventions.
  - Clinicians and health systems should incorporate D&I frameworks when planning and evaluating the implementation of new guidelines or quality improvement initiatives.
  - Multidisciplinary teams that include community partners, patients, and diverse stakeholders are essential for successful D&I efforts.
  - Guideline developers should consider including implementation strategies and D&I principles to facilitate real-world adoption.

Clinical implications:
  - These results reinforce current ARIA Guidelines and the US Practice Parameter recommendations that favor intranasal treatments for moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis, though they should be considered alongside other evidence.

Limitations:
  - D&I studies can be expensive, particularly when multiple sites are involved, and may face competing operational pressures within health systems.
  - The variety of available D&I frameworks can be daunting, and selecting the most appropriate one requires expertise.
  - Without careful integration of a health equity lens, D&I research risks exacerbating existing disparities by favoring populations with greater access and health literacy.
  - The need for mixed methods, longitudinal data, and real-time EHR or digital data collection adds complexity to study design and execution.

Strengths:
  - D&I sciences provide a rigorous, systematic methodology to study not only clinical effectiveness but also reach, adoption, implementation fidelity, and sustainability of evidence-based practices.
  - The use of process, determinant, and evaluation frameworks (e.g., EPIS, CFIR, RE-AIM) offers structured roadmaps to guide implementation and assess contextual factors.
  - Mixed methods approaches allow for a comprehensive understanding of barriers and facilitators at individual, organizational, and system levels.
  - D&I research explicitly prioritizes health equity and can uncover how interventions affect historically marginalized populations differently.

Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

  - How can D&I studies effectively address structural barriers such as insurance coverage and FDA approval status that limit guideline implementation?
  - What strategies are most effective for de-implementing low-value or outdated practices, such as routine corticosteroid use in biphasic anaphylaxis prevention?

Future directions:
  - Increase dedicated grant funding for D&I research in allergy and immunology from agencies such as NIH and PCORI.
  - Develop training and mentorship programs to build D&I science capacity among allergists, immunologists, and researchers.
  - Expand research networks to include implementation scientists and health disparities experts as core collaborators.
  - Integrate D&I considerations directly into the development and dissemination of clinical practice guidelines and practice parameters.
  - Conduct more pragmatic and hybrid effectiveness-implementation trials to accelerate translation of evidence into front-line practice.
  - Leverage D&I approaches to design and test interventions that specifically target health inequities in allergic and immunologic conditions.

Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions

Condition or topic: Allergic rhinitis

Clinical background: Allergic rhinitis is commonly managed with intranasal or oral medications. Current guidelines, such as ARIA 2020, suggest intranasal treatments for moderate-to-severe disease, citing faster onset and higher effectiveness, but the certainty of evidence for these recommendations is often low or very low. Similarly, the US 2020 Practice Parameter recommends intranasal corticosteroids as first-line therapy without detailed comparisons with oral options. Existing head-to-head studies have employed heterogeneous outcome measures and inconsistent methodological rigor. Recent high-quality systematic reviews on this topic are absent; the last comprehensive review was published in 1998 and limited to intranasal corticosteroids versus oral antihistamines, while a later review imposed language and date restrictions. An updated evidence synthesis is required to support the 2024 revision of the ARIA guidelines.

Objectives:
  - To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the effectiveness of intranasal corticosteroids or intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists in improving nasal and ocular symptoms and quality of life in allergic rhinitis.
  - To assess the safety of these interventions by evaluating adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events.

Clinical question: In patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis (P), how do intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) (I) compare with oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists) (C) in improving total nasal symptom score, total ocular symptom score, and rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life (O)?

retrieved_chunks.text: Narrative summary: This systematic review with meta-analysis synthesized data from 35 randomized controlled trials enrolling patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal allergic rhinitis. The review compared intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) against oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists). Outcomes included Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS), Total Ocular Symptom Score (TOSS), Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ), adverse events, and withdrawals due to adverse events. Meta-analyses demonstrated that intranasal corticosteroids were significantly more effective than oral antihistamines for TNSS (MD −0.86; 95% CI −1.21 to −0.51; I² = 70%), TOSS (MD −0.36; 95% CI −0.56 to −0.17; I² = 0%), and RQLQ (MD −0.88; 95% CI −1.15 to −0.61; I² = 0%). Intranasal corticosteroids also outperformed leukotriene receptor antagonists (TNSS MD −1.05; 95% CI −1.33 to −0.77). Intranasal antihistamines were more effective than oral antihistamines for TNSS (MD −0.47; 95% CI −0.81 to −0.14; I² = 0%) and RQLQ (MD −0.31; 95% CI −0.57 to −0.06; I² = 0%). Safety outcomes showed no significant differences between intranasal and oral treatments overall, except for a higher risk of adverse events with intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines (RR 2.10; 95% CI 1.04–4.26). The certainty of evidence was moderate to high for most comparisons. These findings strongly support the preferential use of intranasal medications as first-line therapy for seasonal allergic rhinitis and may inform future guideline recommendations. However, the evidence is limited to seasonal allergic rhinitis; data on perennial disease are sparse.

  - Without careful integration of a health equity lens, D&I research risks exacerbating existing disparities by favoring populations with greater access and health literacy.
  - The need for mixed methods, longitudinal data, and real-time EHR or digital data collection adds complexity to study design and execution.

  - D&I research explicitly prioritizes health equity and can uncover how interventions affect historically marginalized populations differently.

Condition or topic: Allergic rhinitis

Clinical background: Allergic rhinitis is commonly managed with intranasal or oral medications. Current guidelines, such as ARIA 2020, suggest intranasal treatments for moderate-to-severe disease, citing faster onset and higher effectiveness, but the certainty of evidence for these recommendations is often low or very low. Similarly, the US 2020 Practice Parameter recommends intranasal corticosteroids as first-line therapy without detailed comparisons with oral options. Existing head-to-head studies have employed heterogeneous outcome measures and inconsistent methodological rigor. Recent high-quality systematic reviews on this topic are absent; the last comprehensive review was published in 1998 and limited to intranasal corticosteroids versus oral antihistamines, while a later review imposed language and date restrictions. An updated evidence synthesis is required to support the 2024 revision of the ARIA guidelines.

Objectives:
  - To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the effectiveness of intranasal corticosteroids or intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists in improving nasal and ocular symptoms and quality of life in allergic rhinitis.
  - To assess the safety of these interventions by evaluating adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events.

Clinical question: In patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis (P), how do intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) (I) compare with oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists) (C) in improving total nasal symptom score, total ocular symptom score, and rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life (O)?

Intranasal corticosteroids also outperformed leukotriene receptor antagonists (TNSS MD −1.05; 95% CI −1.33 to −0.77). Intranasal antihistamines were more effective than oral antihistamines for TNSS (MD −0.47; 95% CI −0.81 to −0.14; I² = 0%) and RQLQ (MD −0.31; 95% CI −0.57 to −0.06; I² = 0%). The certainty of evidence was moderate to high for most comparisons. These findings strongly support the preferential use of intranasal medications as first-line therapy for seasonal allergic rhinitis and may inform future guideline recommendations. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

Limitations:
  - D&I studies can be expensive, particularly when multiple sites are involved, and may face competing operational pressures within health systems.
  - The variety of available D&I frameworks can be daunting, and selecting the most appropriate one requires expertise.
  - Without careful integration of a health equity lens, D&I research risks exacerbating existing disparities by favoring populations with greater access and health literacy.
  - The need for mixed methods, longitudinal data, and real-time EHR or digital data collection adds complexity to study design and execution.

Strengths:
  - D&I sciences provide a rigorous, systematic methodology to study not only clinical effectiveness but also reach, adoption, implementation fidelity, and sustainability of evidence-based practices.
  - The use of process, determinant, and evaluation frameworks (e.g., EPIS, CFIR, RE-AIM) offers structured roadmaps to guide implementation and assess contextual factors.
  - Mixed methods approaches allow for a comprehensive understanding of barriers and facilitators at individual, organizational, and system levels.
  - D&I research explicitly prioritizes health equity and can uncover how interventions affect historically marginalized populations differently.

Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions

retrieved_chunks.text:
Condition or topic: Ocular allergy, specifically allergic conjunctivitis (seasonal and perennial)

Clinical background: Ocular allergy represents a set of often underappreciated immune-mediated inflammatory conditions affecting the anterior eye surface, encompassing various clinical presentations in both children and adults. Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common form and is sub-classified into seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and perennial allergic conjunctivitis depending on whether the triggering aeroallergen is seasonal or present year-round; grass pollen is the most frequent sensitizer in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, whereas dust mites and animal dander predominate in perennial allergic conjunctivitis. The prevalence of ocular allergy has been rising globally for decades, with seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis affecting between 14% and up to 45% of the general population depending on geographic area. Despite this, allergic conjunctivitis remains underdiagnosed and undertreated—only 10% of affected individuals seek medical attention, with most self-managing using over-the-counter products and non-pharmacological remedies. Ocular allergy frequently coexists with other ocular disorders such as infections and dry eye disease, markedly impairs quality of life, and imposes a substantial economic burden. Management encompasses preventive, non-pharmacological, and pharmacological strategies. First-line pharmacotherapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and agents with dual activity, while corticosteroids and immunomodulators are reserved for severe keratoconjunctivitis. Because many patients receive topical treatments for prolonged periods, the short- and long-term safety and ocular surface tolerability of these preparations are critical; certain excipients in ophthalmic solutions can disrupt the epithelial barrier and tear film, potentially leading to dry eye or exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. The review aims to collate current evidence on these therapeutic options.

Condition or topic: Allergic rhinitis

Clinical background: Allergic rhinitis is commonly managed with intranasal or oral medications. Current guidelines, such as ARIA 2020, suggest intranasal treatments for moderate-to-severe disease, citing faster onset and higher effectiveness, but the certainty of evidence for these recommendations is often low or very low. Similarly, the US 2020 Practice Parameter recommends intranasal corticosteroids as first-line therapy without detailed comparisons with oral options. Existing head-to-head studies have employed heterogeneous outcome measures and inconsistent methodological rigor. Recent high-quality systematic reviews on this topic are absent; the last comprehensive review was published in 1998 and limited to intranasal corticosteroids versus oral antihistamines, while a later review imposed language and date restrictions. An updated evidence synthesis is required to support the 2024 revision of the ARIA guidelines.

Objectives:
  - To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the effectiveness of intranasal corticosteroids or intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists in improving nasal and ocular symptoms and quality of life in allergic rhinitis.
  - To assess the safety of these interventions by evaluating adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events.

Clinical question: In patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis (P), how do intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) (I) compare with oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists) (C) in improving total nasal symptom score, total ocular symptom score, and rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life (O)?

retrieved_chunks.text: Narrative summary: This systematic review with meta-analysis synthesized data from 35 randomized controlled trials enrolling patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal allergic rhinitis. The review compared intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) against oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists). Outcomes included Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS), Total Ocular Symptom Score (TOSS), Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ), adverse events, and withdrawals due to adverse events. Meta-analyses demonstrated that intranasal corticosteroids were significantly more effective than oral antihistamines for TNSS (MD −0.86; 95% CI −1.21 to −0.51; I² = 70%), TOSS (MD −0.36; 95% CI −0.56 to −0.17; I² = 0%), and RQLQ (MD −0.88; 95% CI −1.15 to −0.61; I² = 0%). Intranasal corticosteroids also outperformed leukotriene receptor antagonists (TNSS MD −1.05; 95% CI −1.33 to −0.77). Intranasal antihistamines were more effective than oral antihistamines for TNSS (MD −0.47; 95% CI −0.81 to −0.14; I² = 0%) and RQLQ (MD −0.31; 95% CI −0.57 to −0.06; I² = 0%). Safety outcomes showed no significant differences between intranasal and oral treatments overall, except for a higher risk of adverse events with intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines (RR 2.10; 95% CI 1.04–4.26). The certainty of evidence was moderate to high for most comparisons. These findings strongly support the preferential use of intranasal medications as first-line therapy for seasonal allergic rhinitis and may inform future guideline recommendations. However, the evidence is limited to seasonal allergic rhinitis; data on perennial disease are sparse.

Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions

Condition or topic: Anaphylaxis and innovative epinephrine treatments

Clinical background: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially fatal allergic reaction requiring prompt epinephrine administration. Intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjector (EAI) is the standard outpatient emergency treatment, but barriers such as undercarriage, underuse, needle phobia, and device size lead to delayed administration and increased morbidity. Clinical implications:
  - Needle-free epinephrine products may lower the threshold for patient and caregiver use by reducing needle fear and device bulk, potentially leading to earlier administration.
  - Higher and more sustained epinephrine plasma levels could offer therapeutic advantages, but the clinical significance of elevated Cmax or prolonged exposure remains unproven.
  - Despite promising pharmacokinetics, the surrogate nature of plasma levels limits direct inference about efficacy in real anaphylaxis episodes.

Practice implications:
  - If approved, these novel epinephrine products could become patient-preferred alternatives to autoinjectors, improving carriage and confidence in emergency treatment.
  - Robust education and training on anaphylaxis recognition and management are still essential, regardless of the delivery device used.
  - Healthcare providers should be aware that current evidence is based on healthy volunteer studies and that real-world performance during anaphylaxis is not yet established.

Condition or topic: Hymenoptera venom allergy

Clinical background: Hymenoptera venom allergy represents the leading cause of anaphylaxis among adults and the second most common in children. Stings can provoke reactions ranging from normal local responses to large local reactions and systemic manifestations involving the skin, respiratory tract, cardiovascular system, gastrointestinal tract, or nervous system. European epidemiological data indicate that systemic reactions occur in 0.3 to 8.9% of adults and up to 32% of beekeepers. Although fatalities are uncommon, Hymenoptera stings account for 20% of anaphylaxis-related deaths. Thus, this allergy is potentially life-threatening, and all patients with systemic symptoms require thorough diagnostic evaluation. Accurate diagnosis is essential for appropriate management, including venom immunotherapy (VIT), which is the most effective treatment for reducing the risk of future severe reactions and for improving quality of life. Currently, improved diagnostic tools enable individualized diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.

retrieved_chunks.text: Narrative summary: Current first-line outpatient emergency treatment for anaphylaxis relies on intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjectors (EAIs), but undercarriage and underuse are common due to factors like needle phobia, bulky devices, dosing limitations, and training gaps. This review evaluates human studies on novel nasal and sublingual epinephrine products intended to address these barriers. Data from phase 1 and 2 studies show that several nasal sprays (ARS-1 2 mg, BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg, FMXIN002 3.2 mg, Hikma) and a sublingual film (AQST-109-DESF 12 mg) achieve peak plasma concentrations (Cmax) and times to peak (Tmax) comparable to or better than a 0.3-mg EAI. For example, ARS-1 had a mean Cmax lower than EpiPen but produced comparable or greater blood pressure increases; BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg yielded higher and more sustained plasma levels than the autoinjector; AQST-109 12 mg showed a faster median Tmax of 12 minutes versus variable EAI times. Pharmacodynamic responses, including heart rate and blood pressure changes, were generally similar or more pronounced. Safety profiles were acceptable, with mild and transient adverse events. Importantly, no studies have been conducted during actual anaphylactic episodes, and pediatric data are sparse. Despite these limitations, the portability, ease of use, and needle-free design of these products could encourage earlier epinephrine administration, potentially reducing morbidity and mortality. FDA approval, which hinges on pharmacokinetic equivalence and safety, may soon expand options for patients and caregivers, alleviating key barriers to effective anaphylaxis management.

Limitations:
  - Insufficient evidence on perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) limited the ability to perform meta-analyses for this condition, so findings chiefly apply to SAR.
  - Only a minority of included studies had a low risk of bias; most had unclear risk, and some had high risk, potentially biasing results.
  - Considerable heterogeneity existed in outcome measurement: some studies used nonstandard definitions of TNSS (e.g., 3 or 5 symptoms) or TOSS (2 or 4 symptoms), and the Total Symptom Score (TSS) could not be meta-analyzed due to inconsistent definitions.
  - Missing spread measures in several studies required imputation based on P values, though sensitivity analyses excluding such studies yielded consistent findings.
  - The inability to comprehensively assess the effect of individual drugs within each class, due to the low number of studies per comparison, could mask variability in effectiveness.
  - The overall comparison between intranasal and oral treatments might be influenced by class-specific differences in effectiveness and safety, as well as the proportion of studies assessing each class.
  - The classification of rhinitis as seasonal/perennial rather than intermittent/persistent reflects the design of included RCTs, though the authors believe results may generalize.

Strengths:
  - The systematic review used an extensive search of four bibliographic databases and three clinical trial registries, without restrictions on language, date, or publication status, minimizing publication bias.
  - The GRADE approach was applied to assess certainty of evidence for each outcome across comparisons.
  - Sensitivity analyses were conducted examining risk of bias, imputation of spread measures, follow-up duration, and individual drugs compared.
  - When potential effect modification was identified, the credibility of that modification was assessed using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN).
  - A complementary method was used to evaluate the probability that observed differences corresponded to clinically relevant effects, based on decision thresholds.

Main conclusion: The management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis should prioritize topical therapies that effectively control signs and symptoms while minimizing iatrogenic damage to the ocular surface, as many commercial formulations contain preservatives like benzalkonium chloride that can disrupt the tear film and exacerbate dry eye disease.

Narrative summary: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives. SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease. First-line pharmacological therapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and dual-action agents, with recent additions like bilastine 0.6 mg/ml (preservative-free, once daily, co-formulated with hyaluronic acid) and cetirizine 2.4 mg/ml. However, many older products contain benzalkonium chloride (BAK), a preservative that disrupts the epithelial barrier and may promote dry eye. The review tabulates approved multi-dose formulations, detailing their excipients, dosing, and preservative content. For instance, levocabastine, emedastine, and several dual-action agents contain BAK at varying concentrations, while preservative-free single-dose options exist for ketotifen, olopatadine, and azelastine. Topical vasoconstrictors and NSAIDs are discouraged due to limited efficacy and adverse effects, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases under ophthalmological supervision. Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. In summary, clinicians should select topical agents not only for their antiallergic efficacy but also for their formulation’s impact on the ocular surface, preferentially using preservative-free or low-toxicity preparations to optimize long-term safety and tolerability.

  - Name: Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE)
    Description: Framework for assessing the certainty of evidence in systematic reviews.
  - Name: Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN)
    Description: Tool to evaluate the credibility of subgroup effect modifications in meta-analyses.

Interpretation: The meta-analysis found that intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) or intranasal antihistamines (INAH) are more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) or leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) in improving nasal and ocular symptoms in seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR), as well as quality of life. Most effects were considered clinically relevant. Safety outcomes were generally similar between intranasal and oral treatments, except for a higher risk of adverse events with INAH compared to OAH. The certainty of evidence (CoE) for most comparisons was moderate or high, supporting the reliability of these findings.

Comparison with prior evidence: Previous systematic reviews on this topic were older, assessed fewer drug classes, and restricted study selection based on publication dates or languages. They did not use the GRADE approach to evaluate CoE. However, their results consistently suggested superiority of intranasal over oral medications, aligning with the current findings.

Condition or topic: Anaphylaxis and innovative epinephrine treatments

Clinical background: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially fatal allergic reaction requiring prompt epinephrine administration. Intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjector (EAI) is the standard outpatient emergency treatment, but barriers such as undercarriage, underuse, needle phobia, and device size lead to delayed administration and increased morbidity. Patients and healthcare professionals desire more convenient, needle-free options to improve carriage and ease of use.

Objectives:
  - To review recent data on innovative nasal and oral epinephrine products under investigation for the outpatient emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

Interpretation: The meta-analysis found that intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) or intranasal antihistamines (INAH) are more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) or leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) in improving nasal and ocular symptoms in seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR), as well as quality of life. Most effects were considered clinically relevant. Safety outcomes were generally similar between intranasal and oral treatments, except for a higher risk of adverse events with INAH compared to OAH. The certainty of evidence (CoE) for most comparisons was moderate or high, supporting the reliability of these findings.

Comparison with prior evidence: Previous systematic reviews on this topic were older, assessed fewer drug classes, and restricted study selection based on publication dates or languages. They did not use the GRADE approach to evaluate CoE. However, their results consistently suggested superiority of intranasal over oral medications, aligning with the current findings.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Main conclusion: The management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis should prioritize topical therapies that effectively control signs and symptoms while minimizing iatrogenic damage to the ocular surface, as many commercial formulations contain preservatives like benzalkonium chloride that can disrupt the tear film and exacerbate dry eye disease.

Narrative summary: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives. SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease. First-line pharmacological therapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and dual-action agents, with recent additions like bilastine 0.6 mg/ml (preservative-free, once daily, co-formulated with hyaluronic acid) and cetirizine 2.4 mg/ml. However, many older products contain benzalkonium chloride (BAK), a preservative that disrupts the epithelial barrier and may promote dry eye. The review tabulates approved multi-dose formulations, detailing their excipients, dosing, and preservative content. For instance, levocabastine, emedastine, and several dual-action agents contain BAK at varying concentrations, while preservative-free single-dose options exist for ketotifen, olopatadine, and azelastine. Topical vasoconstrictors and NSAIDs are discouraged due to limited efficacy and adverse effects, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases under ophthalmological supervision. Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. In summary, clinicians should select topical agents not only for their antiallergic efficacy but also for their formulation’s impact on the ocular surface, preferentially using preservative-free or low-toxicity preparations to optimize long-term safety and tolerability.

Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions

Statistical methods: Random-effects meta-analyses of mean differences in change from baseline were performed for effectiveness outcomes. Restricted maximum likelihood was used to estimate between-study variance. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q-Cochran test P value and the I² statistic. Sensitivity analyses were conducted, including exclusion of studies with high risk of bias, imputed standard deviations, or non-2-week follow-up; and analyses restricted to specific drug comparisons. The credibility of effect modification in subgroup analyses was evaluated using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses. A complementary approach computed probabilities of large, moderate, small, or trivial clinically relevant effects. Safety outcomes were meta-analyzed using risk ratios from random-effects models. Certainty of evidence was assessed with the GRADE approach.

Follow up: At least 2 weeks for seasonal allergic rhinitis and at least 4 weeks for perennial allergic rhinitis, based on inclusion criteria.

Population:
  Description: Patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal allergic rhinitis or perennial allergic rhinitis.

    - Patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Limitations:
  - Insufficient evidence on perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) limited the ability to perform meta-analyses for this condition, so findings chiefly apply to SAR.
  - Only a minority of included studies had a low risk of bias; most had unclear risk, and some had high risk, potentially biasing results.
  - Considerable heterogeneity existed in outcome measurement: some studies used nonstandard definitions of TNSS (e.g., 3 or 5 symptoms) or TOSS (2 or 4 symptoms), and the Total Symptom Score (TSS) could not be meta-analyzed due to inconsistent definitions.
  - Missing spread measures in several studies required imputation based on P values, though sensitivity analyses excluding such studies yielded consistent findings.
  - The inability to comprehensively assess the effect of individual drugs within each class, due to the low number of studies per comparison, could mask variability in effectiveness.
  - The overall comparison between intranasal and oral treatments might be influenced by class-specific differences in effectiveness and safety, as well as the proportion of studies assessing each class.
  - The classification of rhinitis as seasonal/perennial rather than intermittent/persistent reflects the design of included RCTs, though the authors believe results may generalize.

Strengths:
  - The systematic review used an extensive search of four bibliographic databases and three clinical trial registries, without restrictions on language, date, or publication status, minimizing publication bias.
  - The GRADE approach was applied to assess certainty of evidence for each outcome across comparisons.
  - Sensitivity analyses were conducted examining risk of bias, imputation of spread measures, follow-up duration, and individual drugs compared.
  - When potential effect modification was identified, the credibility of that modification was assessed using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN).
  - A complementary method was used to evaluate the probability that observed differences corresponded to clinically relevant effects, based on decision thresholds.

Scales and classifications:
  - Name: Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS)
    Description: Patient-reported outcome measuring four nasal symptoms (congestion, itching, sneezing, rhinorrhea); higher score indicates worse symptoms.
  - Name: Total Ocular Symptom Score (TOSS)
    Description: Patient-reported outcome for three ocular symptoms (itching/burning, tearing/watering, redness); higher score indicates worse symptoms.
  - Name: Total Symptom Score (TSS)
    Description: Patient-reported outcome with varying symptom composition across studies; not meta-analyzed due to heterogeneity.
  - Name: Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ)
    Description: Questionnaire measuring quality of life in rhinoconjunctivitis; higher score indicates greater impairment.
  - Name: Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB)
    Description: Instrument to assess risk of bias in randomized controlled trials across several domains.
  - Name: Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE)
    Description: Framework for assessing the certainty of evidence in systematic reviews.
  - Name: Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN)
    Description: Tool to evaluate the credibility of subgroup effect modifications in meta-analyses.
  - Name: ARIA guidelines classification
    Description: Allergic rhinitis classified as seasonal/perennial or intermittent/persistent based on symptom duration and triggers.

Interpretation: The meta-analysis found that intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) or intranasal antihistamines (INAH) are more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) or leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) in improving nasal and ocular symptoms in seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR), as well as quality of life. Most effects were considered clinically relevant. Safety outcomes were generally similar between intranasal and oral treatments, except for a higher risk of adverse events with INAH compared to OAH. The certainty of evidence (CoE) for most comparisons was moderate or high, supporting the reliability of these findings.

Comparison with prior evidence: Previous systematic reviews on this topic were older, assessed fewer drug classes, and restricted study selection based on publication dates or languages. They did not use the GRADE approach to evaluate CoE. However, their results consistently suggested superiority of intranasal over oral medications, aligning with the current findings.

Condition or topic: Anaphylaxis and innovative epinephrine treatments

Clinical background: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially fatal allergic reaction requiring prompt epinephrine administration. Intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjector (EAI) is the standard outpatient emergency treatment, but barriers such as undercarriage, underuse, needle phobia, and device size lead to delayed administration and increased morbidity. Patients and healthcare professionals desire more convenient, needle-free options to improve carriage and ease of use.

Objectives:
  - To review recent data on innovative nasal and oral epinephrine products under investigation for the outpatient emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__paper_PAPER - Lieberman et al. - 2023 - Innovations in the treatment of anaphylaxis A review of recent data__JC__000050
retrieved_chunks.document_id: paper_PAPER - Lieberman et al. - 2023 - Innovations in the treatment of anaphylaxis A review of recent data
retrieved_chunks.text: Narrative summary: Current first-line outpatient emergency treatment for anaphylaxis relies on intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjectors (EAIs), but undercarriage and underuse are common due to factors like needle phobia, bulky devices, dosing limitations, and training gaps. This review evaluates human studies on novel nasal and sublingual epinephrine products intended to address these barriers. Data from phase 1 and 2 studies show that several nasal sprays (ARS-1 2 mg, BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg, FMXIN002 3.2 mg, Hikma) and a sublingual film (AQST-109-DESF 12 mg) achieve peak plasma concentrations (Cmax) and times to peak (Tmax) comparable to or better than a 0.3-mg EAI. For example, ARS-1 had a mean Cmax lower than EpiPen but produced comparable or greater blood pressure increases; BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg yielded higher and more sustained plasma levels than the autoinjector; AQST-109 12 mg showed a faster median Tmax of 12 minutes versus variable EAI times. Pharmacodynamic responses, including heart rate and blood pressure changes, were generally similar or more pronounced. Safety profiles were acceptable, with mild and transient adverse events. Importantly, no studies have been conducted during actual anaphylactic episodes, and pediatric data are sparse. Despite these limitations, the portability, ease of use, and needle-free design of these products could encourage earlier epinephrine administration, potentially reducing morbidity and mortality. FDA approval, which hinges on pharmacokinetic equivalence and safety, may soon expand options for patients and caregivers, alleviating key barriers to effective anaphylaxis management.

Open questions:
  - What is the optimal plasma epinephrine concentration and duration of exposure required to effectively reverse anaphylaxis?
  - Do higher Cmax values or prolonged therapeutic levels translate into clinically meaningful benefits (e.g., reduced hospitalizations, mortality)?
  - What causes the observed pharmacodynamic differences between intranasal/sublingual and intramuscular routes?
  - Which pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic parameters are most predictive of real-world treatment success?
  - How will these products perform in patients during actual anaphylactic reactions, where physiological changes may alter absorption and response?

Future directions:
  - Conduct real-world efficacy studies in patients during anaphylaxis, including pediatric and older adult populations.
  - Perform head-to-head comparative trials among novel products.
  - Evaluate patient and caregiver preferences, ease of use, and actual carriage in everyday settings.
  - Investigate age-related differences in pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic responses.
  - Explore cost-effectiveness and impact on healthcare utilization to support widespread adoption.

Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

Limitations:
  - D&I studies can be expensive, particularly when multiple sites are involved, and may face competing operational pressures within health systems.
  - The variety of available D&I frameworks can be daunting, and selecting the most appropriate one requires expertise.
  - Without careful integration of a health equity lens, D&I research risks exacerbating existing disparities by favoring populations with greater access and health literacy.
  - The need for mixed methods, longitudinal data, and real-time EHR or digital data collection adds complexity to study design and execution.

Strengths:
  - D&I sciences provide a rigorous, systematic methodology to study not only clinical effectiveness but also reach, adoption, implementation fidelity, and sustainability of evidence-based practices.
  - The use of process, determinant, and evaluation frameworks (e.g., EPIS, CFIR, RE-AIM) offers structured roadmaps to guide implementation and assess contextual factors.
  - Mixed methods approaches allow for a comprehensive understanding of barriers and facilitators at individual, organizational, and system levels.
  - D&I research explicitly prioritizes health equity and can uncover how interventions affect historically marginalized populations differently.

Scales and classifications:
  - Name: Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS)
    Description: Patient-reported outcome measuring four nasal symptoms (congestion, itching, sneezing, rhinorrhea); higher score indicates worse symptoms.
  - Name: Total Ocular Symptom Score (TOSS)
    Description: Patient-reported outcome for three ocular symptoms (itching/burning, tearing/watering, redness); higher score indicates worse symptoms.
  - Name: Total Symptom Score (TSS)
    Description: Patient-reported outcome with varying symptom composition across studies; not meta-analyzed due to heterogeneity.
  - Name: Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ)
    Description: Questionnaire measuring quality of life in rhinoconjunctivitis; higher score indicates greater impairment.
  - Name: Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB)
    Description: Instrument to assess risk of bias in randomized controlled trials across several domains.
  - Name: Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE)
    Description: Framework for assessing the certainty of evidence in systematic reviews.
  - Name: Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN)
    Description: Tool to evaluate the credibility of subgroup effect modifications in meta-analyses.
  - Name: ARIA guidelines classification
    Description: Allergic rhinitis classified as seasonal/perennial or intermittent/persistent based on symptom duration and triggers.

Limitations:
  - Insufficient evidence on perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) limited the ability to perform meta-analyses for this condition, so findings chiefly apply to SAR.
  - Only a minority of included studies had a low risk of bias; most had unclear risk, and some had high risk, potentially biasing results.
  - Considerable heterogeneity existed in outcome measurement: some studies used nonstandard definitions of TNSS (e.g., 3 or 5 symptoms) or TOSS (2 or 4 symptoms), and the Total Symptom Score (TSS) could not be meta-analyzed due to inconsistent definitions.
  - Missing spread measures in several studies required imputation based on P values, though sensitivity analyses excluding such studies yielded consistent findings.
  - The inability to comprehensively assess the effect of individual drugs within each class, due to the low number of studies per comparison, could mask variability in effectiveness.
  - The overall comparison between intranasal and oral treatments might be influenced by class-specific differences in effectiveness and safety, as well as the proportion of studies assessing each class.
  - The classification of rhinitis as seasonal/perennial rather than intermittent/persistent reflects the design of included RCTs, though the authors believe results may generalize.

Strengths:
  - The systematic review used an extensive search of four bibliographic databases and three clinical trial registries, without restrictions on language, date, or publication status, minimizing publication bias.
  - The GRADE approach was applied to assess certainty of evidence for each outcome across comparisons.
  - Sensitivity analyses were conducted examining risk of bias, imputation of spread measures, follow-up duration, and individual drugs compared.
  - When potential effect modification was identified, the credibility of that modification was assessed using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN).
  - A complementary method was used to evaluate the probability that observed differences corresponded to clinically relevant effects, based on decision thresholds.

Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions

Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

Limitations:
  - D&I studies can be expensive, particularly when multiple sites are involved, and may face competing operational pressures within health systems.
  - The variety of available D&I frameworks can be daunting, and selecting the most appropriate one requires expertise.
  - Without careful integration of a health equity lens, D&I research risks exacerbating existing disparities by favoring populations with greater access and health literacy.
  - The need for mixed methods, longitudinal data, and real-time EHR or digital data collection adds complexity to study design and execution.

Strengths:
  - D&I sciences provide a rigorous, systematic methodology to study not only clinical effectiveness but also reach, adoption, implementation fidelity, and sustainability of evidence-based practices.
  - The use of process, determinant, and evaluation frameworks (e.g., EPIS, CFIR, RE-AIM) offers structured roadmaps to guide implementation and assess contextual factors.
  - Mixed methods approaches allow for a comprehensive understanding of barriers and facilitators at individual, organizational, and system levels.
  - D&I research explicitly prioritizes health equity and can uncover how interventions affect historically marginalized populations differently.

Statistical methods: Random-effects meta-analyses of mean differences in change from baseline were performed for effectiveness outcomes. Restricted maximum likelihood was used to estimate between-study variance. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q-Cochran test P value and the I² statistic. Sensitivity analyses were conducted, including exclusion of studies with high risk of bias, imputed standard deviations, or non-2-week follow-up; and analyses restricted to specific drug comparisons. The credibility of effect modification in subgroup analyses was evaluated using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses. A complementary approach computed probabilities of large, moderate, small, or trivial clinically relevant effects. Safety outcomes were meta-analyzed using risk ratios from random-effects models. Certainty of evidence was assessed with the GRADE approach.

Follow up: At least 2 weeks for seasonal allergic rhinitis and at least 4 weeks for perennial allergic rhinitis, based on inclusion criteria.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Limitations:
  - Insufficient evidence on perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) limited the ability to perform meta-analyses for this condition, so findings chiefly apply to SAR.
  - Only a minority of included studies had a low risk of bias; most had unclear risk, and some had high risk, potentially biasing results.
  - Considerable heterogeneity existed in outcome measurement: some studies used nonstandard definitions of TNSS (e.g., 3 or 5 symptoms) or TOSS (2 or 4 symptoms), and the Total Symptom Score (TSS) could not be meta-analyzed due to inconsistent definitions.
  - Missing spread measures in several studies required imputation based on P values, though sensitivity analyses excluding such studies yielded consistent findings.
  - The inability to comprehensively assess the effect of individual drugs within each class, due to the low number of studies per comparison, could mask variability in effectiveness.
  - The overall comparison between intranasal and oral treatments might be influenced by class-specific differences in effectiveness and safety, as well as the proportion of studies assessing each class.
  - The classification of rhinitis as seasonal/perennial rather than intermittent/persistent reflects the design of included RCTs, though the authors believe results may generalize.

Strengths:
  - The systematic review used an extensive search of four bibliographic databases and three clinical trial registries, without restrictions on language, date, or publication status, minimizing publication bias.
  - The GRADE approach was applied to assess certainty of evidence for each outcome across comparisons.
  - Sensitivity analyses were conducted examining risk of bias, imputation of spread measures, follow-up duration, and individual drugs compared.
  - When potential effect modification was identified, the credibility of that modification was assessed using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN).
  - A complementary method was used to evaluate the probability that observed differences corresponded to clinically relevant effects, based on decision thresholds.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Statistical methods: Random-effects meta-analyses of mean differences in change from baseline were performed for effectiveness outcomes. Restricted maximum likelihood was used to estimate between-study variance. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q-Cochran test P value and the I² statistic. Sensitivity analyses were conducted, including exclusion of studies with high risk of bias, imputed standard deviations, or non-2-week follow-up; and analyses restricted to specific drug comparisons. The credibility of effect modification in subgroup analyses was evaluated using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses. A complementary approach computed probabilities of large, moderate, small, or trivial clinically relevant effects. Safety outcomes were meta-analyzed using risk ratios from random-effects models. Certainty of evidence was assessed with the GRADE approach.

Follow up: At least 2 weeks for seasonal allergic rhinitis and at least 4 weeks for perennial allergic rhinitis, based on inclusion criteria.

Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

Main conclusion: The dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences provide essential frameworks to study and enhance the translation of evidence-based practices into real-world allergy and immunology care, promoting health equity and optimizing clinical outcomes through multidisciplinary collaboration and mixed-methods approaches.

Narrative summary: This work group report from the AAAAI Quality, Adherence, and Outcomes Committee examines the role of dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences in allergy and immunology. Despite significant research investment, less than 50% of discoveries reach practice, with an average 17-year lag. D&I sciences use frameworks like EPIS, PRISM, and RE-AIM to systematically identify barriers and facilitators to adopting evidence-based practices. The report emphasizes the need for multidisciplinary teams, mixed-methods data, and stakeholder engagement from the outset. Key examples include school-based asthma programs, penicillin allergy delabeling, early peanut introduction, and SMART therapy for asthma. D&I sciences also offer tools to address health disparities by studying contextual factors and promoting equitable access to interventions. Allergists and immunologists are encouraged to incorporate D&I principles to accelerate the uptake of guidelines into practice, ensuring interventions are effective, sustainable, and equitable. Future directions include increased funding, training, and collaboration with implementation scientists to bridge the evidence-to-practice gap.

Condition or topic: dissemination and implementation sciences in allergy and immunology

Clinical background: Translating evidence-based practices into real-world clinical settings is often slow and resource-intensive. In allergy and immunology, variations in knowledge, resources, patient populations, and staffing models lead to differences in care for asthma, allergic diseases, and primary immunodeficiency. Despite the need for validated approaches to study how to best apply evidence-based practices in the real world, dissemination and implementation (D&I) sciences are underutilized. Uptake of research innovations into clinical practice is low, with less than 50% of discoveries reaching real-world settings and a typical 17-year time lag. Adherence to clinical guidelines in allergy and immunology is variable and influenced by resource availability, preexisting health inequities, clinician preferences, and environmental factors.

Objectives:
  - To provide an overview of the role of dissemination and implementation sciences in clinical care and future research within allergy and immunology
  - To advocate for greater awareness and understanding of D&I sciences as distinct fields of study compared to quality improvement, practice improvement, health services research, and guideline development
  - To provide examples of where D&I sciences can improve care for patients with allergic and immunologic conditions
